holding_summary: The court held that under the Liquor Tax Law a 'hotel' must meet the statutory structural requirements (minimum bedrooms with independent access, dining and kitchen capacity, etc.) and that this status is judged as of the date of the license application. Relator's building failed to meet those requirements and had itself never been operated as a hotel, so his liquor-tax certificate was properly refused while a rival hotel meeting the statute was upheld.

quotes.text: the term ‘ hotel ’ as used in this chapter shall mean a building regularly used and kept open as such for the feeding and lodging of guests, where all who conduct themselves properly and who are able and ready to pay for their entertainment, are received if there be accommodations for them, and who, without any stipulated engagement as to the duration of their stay, or as to the rate of compensation, are, while there, supplied, at a reasonable charge, with their meals, lodgings, refreshment and such service and attention as are necessarily incident to the use of the place as a temporary home, and in which the only other dwellers shall be the family and servants of the hotel keeper;
It clearly appears from the evidence that the relator’s building does not comply with the statutory requirements of a hotel.
The question whether this building complies with the law in respect to its structural requirements for use as a hotel must be determined as of the time when the application for a license was made.

holding_summary: To induce plaintiff's purchase of an adjoining restaurant, the neighboring owners executed a sealed covenant not to rent or themselves use their premises for restaurant or rooming house purposes for ten years. The court held that parol evidence of an alleged unwritten condition (that plaintiff buy his groceries from the covenantors) could not vary the sealed instrument, and gave plaintiff judgment enforcing the restrictive covenant.

quotes.text: it is hereby agreed that the said parties of the first part will not rent the premises located at No. 1675 Broadway, Buffalo, N. Y., or themselves use for restaurant or rooming house purposes for a period of ten years.
The plaintiff must have judgment restraining the violation of defendants’ agreement.

notes: A private sealed covenant, not police-power regulation, but it treats prospective rooming-house use as a commercial-type intrusion worth contractually barring alongside restaurant use -- classified adverse on that basis. who_was_letting/duration left unclear because no actual letting occurred; the dispute concerns a covenant restricting future use, not adjudicated facts of an occupancy.
